summary: Worker A incremental, source-attributed Thymus vulgaris taxonomy, EMA preparation-specific medicinal profiles, clinical uncertainty, two historic metaphysical subprofiles, sample-specific oil constituents, one in-vitro oil assay, product safety and non-prescriptive age/route context. Not a complete dossier; v1.7 nested extraction/media schemas remain unimplemented.
research_method: Primary regulator and taxonomic references, peer-reviewed analytical and in-vitro papers, source-labelled secondary cultural histories; source links inspected 2026-10-17; no original specimens, raw assays or clinical papers independently reproduced.

organisms.accepted_name_authority: Thymus vulgaris L. (Kew POWO accepted, originally published 1753)
organisms.native_range: SW Europe and SE Italy; Kew lists Baleares, France, Italy and Spain as native and many other territories as introduced.
organisms.morphology: Aromatic evergreen dwarf subshrub, often to ~30 cm, with small linear-to-ovate grey-green leaves and white/pink whorled flowers in early summer; cultivar and environment variation.
organisms.identification_cautions: Common name 'thyme' covers multiple Thymus species; EMA Thymi herba and oil also include T. zygis. Species, plant part and chemotype must be confirmed before extrapolating chemistry or product safety; RHS cultivar traits do not guarantee wild identity.
organisms.geographic_context: Native southwestern Europe and southeastern Italy; widely cultivated and introduced elsewhere (Kew POWO).
organisms.part_and_preparation_note: Leaves and flowering tops used as culinary/herbal material; dried herba, expressed juice, extracts and steam-distilled essential oil are distinct materials. Oil chemotypes vary markedly.

occurrences.note: Measured volatile constituent in a particular thymol-chemotype essential-oil sample: 47.1% thymol in Richerenches (France); not a species-wide concentration or an amount in brewed tea.
occurrences.plant_part: essential oil from plant material; precise input part for this sample not established by this record

occurrences.note: Reported among volatile components of T. vulgaris essential oil; relative amounts vary with chemotype; no species-wide percentage is justified.
Measured at 20.1% in the Richerenches (France) thymol-chemotype essential oil; batch-specific GC-MS profile, not universal.
Reported as a volatile constituent in T. vulgaris essential oil; amounts are chemotype/sample dependent.

medicinal_materials.part: Leaves and flowers / above-ground herb (EMA also covers T. zygis)
medicinal_materials.preparation: Dried comminuted herb for herbal tea; expressed juice and liquid/soft/dry solvent extracts are separately described in EMA monograph.
medicinal_materials.processing: Drying/comminution, expression or solvent extraction depending on preparation; no method-specific yield or purity stated in this source.
medicinal_materials.limitations: EMA monograph covers both T. vulgaris and T. zygis, and multiple distinct preparations. No one-to-one efficacy or dosage equivalence across preparations; no extraction yield verified.

medicinal_materials.part: Fresh flowering aerial parts (EMA also covers T. zygis)
medicinal_materials.preparation: Steam-distilled thyme essential oil (Thymi aetheroleum); finished oral, topical and bath products are distinct.
medicinal_materials.processing: Steam distillation of fresh flowering aerial material; source provides method class but not sample-specific yield, recovery or purity.
medicinal_materials.limitations: EMA oil monograph applies to defined preparations of either T. vulgaris or T. zygis; commercial oils differ in chemotype and quality. Essential oil is not interchangeable with tea, raw plant or isolated thymol; do not ingest unformulated oil.

practice_claims.tradition: European Medicines Agency HMPC traditional-use assessment
framework: herb preparation and age-specific product distinctions

framework_details.materia_medica: Dried/comminuted leaves and flowers, expressed juice or defined extracts; EMA also accepts Thymus zygis.
framework_details.indications: Traditional relief of productive cough associated with a cold.
framework_details.route: Oral herbal tea, liquid or solid products as specifically formulated.
framework_details.contraindications: Allergy to thyme or other Lamiaceae; stomach complaints possible.
framework_details.interpretation: HMPC classification is traditional use; clinical efficacy is not established by this classification.

practice_claims.condition_or_goal: Traditional relief of productive/chesty cough with colds.
practice_claims.plant_part: Leaves and flowers; not essential oil
practice_claims.preparation: Dried/comminuted herb, expressed juice or specified soft/liquid/dry extracts
practice_claims.limitations: The monograph also covers T. zygis and product-specific formulations. HMPC reports insufficient clinical evidence for firm efficacy conclusions; no universal dosage or self-treatment advice.

practice_claims.tradition: European Medicines Agency HMPC thyme oil traditional-use assessment

framework_details.materia_medica: Steam-distilled essential oil from fresh flowering aerial parts; EMA also includes T. zygis.
framework_details.indications: Traditional use for symptoms of productive cough/colds in specified medicinal products.
framework_details.route: Oral formulated liquids (adults); topical preparations (adults); bath products (some ages >3 years).
framework_details.contraindications: Thyme oil allergy, possible skin irritation; no facial application; special hot-bath contraindications.
framework_details.interpretation: Traditional-use assessment is not proof of clinical effectiveness or evidence that raw essential oil can safely be swallowed.

practice_claims.condition_or_goal: Traditional symptomatic relief of cough and colds in defined thyme-oil medicines.
practice_claims.preparation: Defined thyme essential-oil medicinal products, not neat oil
practice_claims.limitations: Age/route restrictions differ; steam-distilled oil is distinct from tea and isolated thymol. HMPC judged evidence insufficient for confirmed clinical efficacy.

practice_claims.tradition: EMA HMPC evidence review of human cough study
practice_claims.condition_or_goal: Assess comparative effect on productive cough in adults.
practice_claims.plant_part: Thyme preparation; formulation insufficiently described in reviewed study
practice_claims.preparation: Unspecified thyme preparation compared with bromhexine in 60 adults; not assignable to specific oil or chemotype
practice_claims.limitations: HMPC reports no significant difference between groups, but sample size and inadequate formulation description preclude firm efficacy or equivalence conclusions. Original study not independently extracted in this batch.

practice_claims.tradition: 12th-century Hildegard of Bingen, Physica, as discussed by Metropolitan Museum of Art
practice_claims.condition_or_goal: Historical warming/drying humoral interpretation and ointment/steam-bath use.
practice_claims.plant_part: Thyme herb; historical term may not map uniquely to modern species
practice_claims.preparation: Historical ointment and steam-bath descriptions, not modern treatment instructions
practice_claims.limitations: Museum explicitly cautions Hildegard's 'thymus' may be modern T. vulgaris, not authenticated. Historical claims about leprosy, palsy, lice or eye conditions are NOT clinically verified; no medical directions should be inferred.

folklore.tradition: Ancient Greek symbolism as summarized in UC Davis Nutritional Geography
folklore.region: Ancient Greece / modern secondary historical summary
folklore.theme: Courage, social grace and incense symbolism
folklore.description: UC Davis recounts thyme as historically associated with courage and graceful elegance, and discusses an incense/sacrifice-related Greek etymological association. This is a historical cultural interpretation, not an empirically measurable energetic effect.
folklore.limitations: Secondary educational summary; primary ancient-language and ritual texts not yet independently checked. Do not universalize across all Greek traditions or imply spiritual/clinical proof.

folklore.tradition: Roman classical herbal symbolism as summarized in UC Davis Nutritional Geography
folklore.region: Ancient Rome / modern secondary historical summary
folklore.description: UC Davis reports a historical Roman association of thyme with Venus. Record as a source-specific cultural correspondence, not a general botanical fact or proof of any physiological effect.
folklore.limitations: Secondary summary only; exact ancient text, dating and plant-species identification remain unverified. Not a universally accepted planetary assignment.

regulatory_status.preparation_scope: Thymi herba; defined herb/juice/extract preparations of T. vulgaris or T. zygis
regulatory_status.status_text: HMPC concluded long-standing traditional use for productive cough associated with colds; not well-established clinical efficacy. National authorities assess individual product authorizations.
regulatory_status.limitations: Not blanket EU approval of all thyme products, extracts or claims.

regulatory_status.category: European herbal monograph and EU list entry (traditional use)
regulatory_status.preparation_scope: Steam-distilled oil of fresh flowering aerial parts from T. vulgaris or T. zygis; specific oral/topical/bath medicines
regulatory_status.status_text: HMPC traditional-use conclusions and route-specific cautions; a 2026 scientific-data review call is shown on EMA site, not a replacement final monograph.
regulatory_status.limitations: No claim that undiluted essential oil is safe to ingest or that every marketed oil is licensed.

dose_guidance.preparation: EMA-covered herb, juice or extracts; exact product varies
dose_guidance.population: Generally adults/adolescents older than twelve years; only certain formulations for children older than four years per EMA summary
dose_guidance.intended_use: Traditional productive cough associated with colds
dose_guidance.amount_text: No universal safe amount across preparations; follow the specific authorized product monograph/leaflet, not a general herb dose.
dose_guidance.upper_limit_status: No single safe maximum established by this summary.
dose_guidance.contraindications: Allergy to thyme or other Lamiaceae; seek care if cough persists beyond a week or worsens.
dose_guidance.risks: Stomach complaints possible. Traditional use does not establish safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding, chronic disease or all ages.

dose_guidance.tradition: EU HMPC thyme-oil traditional-use product context
dose_guidance.preparation: Steam-distilled oil in finished medicinal products, NOT neat oil
dose_guidance.route: Defined oral/topical medicines for adults; bath products may have a different age scope
dose_guidance.population: EMA: oral/topical adult-only; some bath products for children older than three years
dose_guidance.amount_text: No universal safe amount across routes or chemotypes; do not infer a dose from raw essential oil.
dose_guidance.upper_limit_status: No universally safe maximum established for concentrated oil.
dose_guidance.contraindications: Oil allergy, skin irritation; no facial application; avoid hot baths with open wounds, acute skin disease, severe infection/fever, serious circulatory or cardiac conditions as detailed by EMA.
dose_guidance.risks: Concentrated oil is not equivalent to herbal tea; do not self-administer undiluted oil or use adult product directions for children.

safety.alert: EMA Thymi herba: contraindicated for patients allergic to thyme or Lamiaceae; stomach upset possible. A cold-associated cough lasting over one week or worsening warrants medical evaluation. Product age restrictions apply.

EMA Thymi aetheroleum: allergic reactions and skin irritation reported; not for facial application; full hot baths contraindicated with open wounds, serious skin disease, fever/severe infection, circulatory disorders, high blood pressure or heart failure. Finished products have route-specific age limits.

bioactivities.target_taxon: Staphylococcus aureus and Brochothrix thermosphacta (food-associated bacterial isolates)
bioactivities.life_stage: Cultured vegetative bacteria; specific strains and stage details not resolved in this summary
bioactivities.study_model: In-vitro antibacterial testing of four GC-MS/GC-FID-characterized thyme oil chemotypes (Schmidt et al. 2012)
bioactivities.endpoint: Antibacterial activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative cultured bacteria
bioactivities.observed_effect: All four tested chemotype oils showed stronger antibacterial activity against Gram-positive strains than against tested Gram-negative bacteria.
bioactivities.mechanism_status: Mechanism not demonstrated by this study abstract; chemical composition correlation is not target binding.
bioactivities.dose_translation: No human dose or treatment efficacy can be inferred from bacterial culture tests.
bioactivities.limitations: In vitro results only; chemotypes differed markedly and no general clinical antibiotic effect is established. Specific assay concentrations not extracted from full paper; no numeric potency claimed.
